transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me, doctor. It’s, uh, it's a bit hard to explain exactly, but I suppose it started becoming a real bother to me recently. You see, since I stopped working—I’ve got a lot more time on my hands these days, mostly just puttering around the house—my evenings can get very long and quiet. My routine is usually to have my dinner, wash the dishes, and pack everything away neatly into the fridge. But then, late at night, maybe around eleven or midnight when the house is completely still and I'm just watching television or reading, I find myself wandering back into the kitchen. 

And I think what really brings me in today is that once I start picking at the leftovers late at night... it’s like a switch flips in my head. I’ll open a container, maybe some cold chicken or some rice, just intending to have one little bite. Just a taste, you know? But once I start, it feels like the sensible part of me is standing right there, clear as day, saying, "That’s enough, Alejandro. You already ate, you don't need this, just close the door and go to bed." I hear that voice in my head so clearly. But my hand just keeps going back for more anyway. It’s the strangest thing, like my hand has a mind of its own, just reaching in, taking another bite, and then another, even while I'm telling myself to stop. I'll just stand there in the light of the refrigerator, picking and picking, and I just can't seem to make myself walk away when I know I should.
Do you usually feel stressed, anxious, or upset before these late-night eating episodes?

Stressed? No, I... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it’s quite the opposite, if you can believe it. You see, since I retired—and I worked for, oh, thirty-five years, always on the go, always some deadline or someone needing something from me—but now? Now there’s really nothing to be stressed about. The house is quiet, the bills are sorted. My evenings are... well, they’re incredibly peaceful. 

I usually just sit in my favorite armchair, it's this old leather one right by the window, and I might put on a history program or read a bit of whatever biography I've picked up from the library. I’m completely relaxed. Not upset, not anxious, not pacing the floors worrying about tomorrow. I just feel... calm. Maybe a little too calm, if that makes any sense? It’s just very quiet. 

So, no, I don't feel upset or nervous before I get up and walk into the kitchen. I’m just sitting there, perfectly content, maybe just a little bored with whatever is on the television, and then I just... wander in there. It’s never because I’m upset about something that happened during the day, because, frankly, my days are very slow and pleasant now. I just don't have those kinds of worries anymore, which makes it all the more confusing why I do this, you know? I'm just sitting there feeling fine, and then the next thing I know, I'm at the fridge again.
Do you feel guilty after these late-night eating episodes?

Guilty? Hmm. I... well, I don't know if I would use the word guilty, exactly. When I think of guilt, you know, I think about doing something wrong to somebody else. Like back when I was working, if I missed a deadline and caused a headache for the people in my department, or, oh, if I forget to call my sister on her birthday—that sort of thing makes me feel terribly guilty. But with this, it is just me in my own kitchen. I bought the groceries, it is my house, I am not taking food out of anyone else's mouth. So, no, I wouldn't say guilt. 

It is more just... well, it is a profound sense of bafflement, really. I will finish picking at whatever it is, and I will put the lid back on the container. I always make sure to press all the corners down tight, because there is nothing worse than refrigerator air drying out the leftovers, and then I will wash whatever fork or spoon I used. I always wash it and dry it right then and there, put it back in the drawer, and wipe down the counter with a sponge. And while I am doing all that tidying up, I just ask myself why on earth I just did that. 

I feel a bit foolish, I suppose. And, well, maybe a little physically heavy, because my stomach was already perfectly satisfied from my actual dinner. But I don't feel guilty like I have committed a crime. I just turn off the kitchen light, walk down the hall to my bedroom, and lay there in the dark for a while, just wondering why my brain and my hands do not seem to be on the same page. It is just so nonsensical, you know? I just go to sleep feeling completely confused about the whole routine.
Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start with the leftovers, even if you want to?

Yes, exactly. That is—well, like I was trying to explain when I first sat down, that is really the crux of the whole issue for me. It is exactly that feeling. I’ll be standing there—usually I’m just in my pajamas and these old blue slippers my daughter got me, the ones with the thick rubber soles so I don't slip on the kitchen linoleum—and I'll have the container open. And I *do* want to stop. I really do. 

It’s not like I'm sleepwalking or in some kind of daze, you know? I am wide awake, the refrigerator light is shining right on me, the house is dead quiet, and I am actively thinking to myself, 'Alejandro, put the lid back on. You don't even want this cold chicken. You are perfectly full.' I hear that sensible voice in my head so clearly, telling me to just shut the door. 

But then... well, it's just like I said before, my hand just reaches back in anyway. It's the most baffling disconnect between my brain and my body. I tell myself to stop, I genuinely want to just close the fridge and go back to my armchair or get into bed, but I just keep taking another bite, and then another. It's like the brakes are completely out on a car, even though I'm slamming my foot down on the pedal, if that makes any sense. I just cannot seem to make myself pull my hand away and walk out of the kitchen, no matter how much I tell myself that I should.
Would you say that during these late-night eating episodes, you're eating a large amount of food in a short period of time?

Well, yes, I suppose it is a large amount, especially when you consider I've already had a full dinner just a few hours prior. It’s... well, it happens when I’m supposed to be putting things away, you see. My wife, Maria, she’s a wonderful cook, and she always makes enough to feed an army, even though it’s just the two of us most nights now that the kids are grown and out of the house. 

So, after supper, it’s my job to pack up the leftovers. I’ll get out the Tupperware—we have this whole drawer full of it, none of the lids ever seem to match the bottoms, which is a whole other frustration—but I’ll be standing there in the kitchen, getting ready to pack away the tamales or the mole she made. And instead of just putting them in the container and sliding them onto the middle shelf of the fridge, I... well, I start eating them. 

And it’s not just a bite or two to taste it, either. I’ll end up eating several full servings, right there standing at the counter. And then, well, it doesn't stop there. I’ll usually go out to the garage—we have a little extra pantry shelf out there where we keep the baked goods so they don't take up space in the kitchen—and I’ll get into the pan dulce. I’ll eat three or four of those sweet breads, just standing out there by my workbench, in the cold, next to the lawnmower. 

When I really stop and think about it, the sheer volume of it all... I mean, I am eating far, far more in those twenty minutes than I would ever, *ever* put on a plate if my family was sitting there watching me. If my daughter came over for dinner, I’d have one tamale, maybe some rice and beans, and that would be it. I’d be perfectly satisfied. But when I’m alone, packing things up, I just keep eating and eating, way past the point of being full, and it’s just an embarrassing amount of food, quite frankly.
Do you feel like you're losing control over what you're eating during these episodes?

Well, yes, absolutely. I think... I mean, I know I've touched on this already, but it really is the heart of the matter. When I'm standing there, packing away Maria's cooking, or when I wander out to the garage for the pan dulce, it's like I'm watching myself do it from a few feet away. I'm completely aware of what's happening. The sensible part of my brain, the Alejandro who knows better, who knows I just had a wonderful dinner and my stomach is perfectly content, that part of me is practically shouting, 'That's enough, Alejandro. Put the lid on. Go wash your hands and sit down.' 

I hear it as plain as day. But my hands... they just don't listen. They just keep going back for more, opening another container, tearing off another piece of sweet bread. It's not that I'm hungry, and it's not that I even really want to be eating it at that moment. It's just this... this compulsion, this complete loss of the steering wheel, if you will. I'm in the driver's seat, my eyes are on the road, but the car is just doing whatever it wants. It’s like the connection between my rational mind and my physical actions is just severed for those twenty minutes. I want to stop, I tell myself to stop, but I just keep eating anyway. That's really what brought me in to see you, to be honest. That feeling of just not being in charge of my own hands anymore.
How often do these late-night eating episodes happen?

Well, let me think about that. It’s funny you ask, because I was actually just trying to figure that out myself the other day while I was out in the garden. I was pruning the rose bushes—Maria loves those yellow roses, the ones by the front gate, though they’re a menace to keep trimmed—and I was just reflecting on how often I’ve been finding myself out in the garage with the pan dulce. 

If I really look back at it, these late-night leftover episodes... they've been happening at least once most weeks. Sometimes it’s two nights a week. And it really all started, or at least got this frequent, since my cousin Hector moved in with us. He had some trouble with his landlord, a whole mess with a leaky roof that never got fixed, so we told him he could take the spare room until he gets back on his feet. He’s family, you know? You don't turn family away. 

But ever since he got here, the dynamic in the house has just shifted. He’s a night owl, always up watching the television, and the volume is just a little too loud, even though he tries to keep it down. So I find myself staying up later, too, just kind of lingering in the kitchen after Maria goes to bed. And that’s when I start packing up the food, and Hector is in the living room, and the house feels different, and before I know it, I’m eating the tamales again. So, yes, I'd say once or twice a week, pretty consistently, ever since Hector brought his boxes over. It’s just become this strange, frustrating routine that I can't seem to break out of, no matter how much I tell myself I won't do it tonight.
Do you feel ashamed of yourself after these late-night eating episodes?

Ashamed... well, I don't know. I really don't know if I'd use that exact word. I know I mentioned earlier that the amount I eat is embarrassing, but shame... shame feels like such a heavy, dark word, doesn't it? Like I've committed some terrible sin or a crime. I don't feel like a criminal in my own kitchen, I just... well, I feel profoundly frustrated with myself, I suppose. 

I'll be standing there, looking down at the empty Tupperware—usually the one with the blue lid, because Maria always uses the blue-lidded ones for the heavy sauces like the mole so they don't stain the clear plastic—and I just look at it and think, 'Alejandro, what on earth are you doing?' It’s more of a complete bafflement. A real annoyance. I mean, I worked for nearly forty years managing logistics down at the shipping yard, keeping track of hundreds of moving parts, making sure every crate was exactly where it needed to be, right on schedule. I was a man who prided himself on discipline and order. 

So to find myself standing out in the cold garage, brushing pan dulce crumbs off my flannel shirt in the dark so my cousin Hector doesn't see them if he happens to walk out to use the washing machine... I don't know if I'd call it shame, exactly, but it is certainly a massive blow to my pride. It just doesn't make any sense to me. I do try to wash the containers quietly and put them in the drying rack before I go to bed, just so Maria doesn't wake up and see that all the leftovers are gone, but that's mostly because I just don't want her to worry or think she needs to cook even more food for us. So, I don't know if I have that deep feeling of shame you're talking about, or if it's just this intense irritation that I can't seem to manage my own two hands when the sun goes down.
Do you feel like you're eating really fast during these late-night episodes?

Fast? Well, you know, I haven't really stopped to think about the speed of it. It's an interesting question, though. When I'm out there in the garage, or standing by the counter with the blue-lidded Tupperware, the whole experience is just so... so strange. I've told you how it feels like I'm watching myself do it, like I'm not really the one in the driver's seat, even though my hands are the ones moving the food to my mouth. 

But as for how fast I'm eating... I really couldn't say. I don't think I'm shoveling it in like a man who hasn't seen a meal in three days, if that's what you mean. I mean, Maria's cooking is something to be savored, usually. Her mole, the way she toasts the chilies and grinds the chocolate... it takes her hours, sometimes a whole afternoon, just to get the balance right. You don't just inhale something that took that much care to prepare. Even the pan dulce, the conchas with the pink sugar topping, I usually like to break off a piece and have it with my coffee in the morning, taking my time with it while I read the paper. 

So when these episodes happen at night, with Hector watching his programs in the other room... I don't know that I'm racing through it. It's more about the sheer volume, the fact that I just keep going and going until the container is empty, rather than trying to beat some sort of clock. I'm just standing there, feeling that frustration I mentioned, wondering why I can't just put the lid back on. But the actual pace of the eating? I really haven't paid much attention to whether it's fast or slow. It just feels... relentless, I suppose is the best word for it. It just keeps happening until it's gone.
Do you feel distressed after these episodes, like something is wrong with your behavior?

Distressed... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly the word for it. It's a very heavy feeling, you know? Like I said earlier about the frustration, it just... it sits with me. 

I'll be standing there in the garage, the washing machine humming quietly in the corner—it’s an older model, a Maytag, we’ve had it for maybe fifteen years and it still runs like a top, though it makes this slight rattling noise during the spin cycle that I’ve been meaning to look into. But anyway, I'll be standing there, and the last of the pan dulce is gone, and I look down at my hands, and this overwhelming sense of... of distress just washes over me. 

It’s not just that I ate too much. It’s this deep, unsettling feeling that something is fundamentally wrong with how I'm acting. I mean, I’m sixty-five years old. I should be well past the age of sneaking around my own house like a teenager trying to hide a bad report card. I spent my whole life being the responsible one, the one who planned the routes, the one who made sure the bills were paid on time, the one who fixed the leaky faucet before it became a real problem. And now, I can't even stop myself from eating a whole tray of tamales when I'm not even hungry. 

It just feels so out of character. It’s distressing because it doesn't align with who I know myself to be. I'll go back inside, quietly lock the door behind me so it doesn't click too loudly and wake Maria, and I'll just lie there in bed staring at the ceiling fan—we keep it on low, even in the winter, just to keep the air moving—and I just turn it over and over in my mind. Why did I do that? What is wrong with me that I can't just go to sleep like a normal person? It’s a very distressing loop to be caught in, Doctor. It really is. It makes me feel like I'm losing my grip on the steering wheel, if that makes sense.
Do you feel a sense of pleasure or euphoria while you're eating during these late-night episodes?

Pleasure? Euphoria? Oh, no, no. I wouldn't say that at all. It's funny you use the word euphoria, actually. It makes me think of... well, years ago, when I was still working down at the shipping yard, we had this young fellow, maybe twenty-two, who won a scratch-off lottery ticket on his lunch break. Won about five thousand dollars, if I recall correctly. Now, that boy was euphoric. He was jumping up and down, buying everyone sodas from the machine in the breakroom—the old machine that always ate your quarters if you didn't push the button fast enough. That's euphoria. 

But what I'm doing out there in the garage, or standing in the kitchen in the dark? There's no joy in it. No pleasure. I mean, the food tastes good, of course. Maria is a wonderful cook. Her tamales, the ones she makes for Christmas with the pork shoulder she slow-roasts all day... they're delicious. And the pan dulce from the bakery down on 4th Street, the one with the green awning that's been there since before Hector and I were born—it's sweet, it's comforting. But when I'm eating it during these... these episodes, I'm not enjoying it. I'm not savoring it like I would if I were sitting at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning with a hot cup of coffee and the newspaper spread out in front of me.

It's more like... like a compulsion, I suppose. A drive. I'm just putting it in my mouth, chewing, swallowing, reaching for the next piece. I'm not thinking about the flavor or the texture. I'm not feeling happy or satisfied. If anything, it's just this dull, numbing sensation. Like I'm just trying to fill a hole, or quiet some sort of noise in my head, though I couldn't tell you what that noise is. It's just... I just have to do it, and I can't seem to stop until it's gone. And then, like I was saying before, the distress sets in. The frustration. But during the actual eating? No, doctor, there's no pleasure in it. It's just a mechanical, relentless sort of thing. I wish I could say it was enjoyable, at least then maybe it would make a little more sense to me, why I keep doing it. But it's not. It really isn't.
Do you think eating at night helps you cope with any emotions or feelings you might be having?

Coping with emotions... well, you see, that's the thing that really stumps me about all of this. If you had asked me that back when I was still working down at the shipping yard—oh, say, fifteen or twenty years ago, right around the time they brought in all that new management and completely overhauled the scheduling system—I might have said yes. Back then, there was plenty of stress to go around. You'd come home with your shoulders pulled tight up to your ears, just completely worn down by the demands of the day and the foremen yelling over the noise of the machinery. 

But now? I'm sixty-five years old, Doctor. I'm retired. My days are... well, they're very peaceful, mostly. I get up, I have my coffee, Maria and I might go down to the market, or I'll spend some time tinkering out in the garage. Just last week I finally got around to replacing the spark plug on the lawnmower. It’s a Toro, a very reliable machine usually, but it gets a bit temperamental if it sits too long over the winter without being run. It took me a good hour to get it cleaned up and running smooth again. But anyway, the point I'm trying to make is that I don't really have a lot of... of turmoil in my life right now. 

I'm not sad. I'm not angry about anything. Hector and I get along just fine, even if he does play his television programs a bit too loud in the evenings—he's a little hard of hearing in his left ear from his time in the service, though you can't ever get him to admit it or go to a doctor for it. Life is good. So I don't feel like I'm trying to cope with anything when I'm out there eating. There's no big sadness or worry that I'm trying to push down with the food. 

When I'm standing there in the dark, I'm not thinking about my feelings at all. It's only after the fact that the emotions really hit me, that terrible distress and frustration I was telling you about earlier. But before it happens? Or during? I really haven't noticed any particular feeling or stress I'm trying to manage. It's just... a blank, really. I wish I could say, "Yes, Doctor, I'm stressed about the bills, and that's why I'm eating," because then at least it would make some logical sense. But I just don't see a connection like that.
Do you think you're eating at night because you're bored or don't know what else to do?

Boredom? Oh, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it's a perfectly fair question, I suppose, what with me being retired and all. I know a lot of fellows, when they finally leave the workforce, they just sort of deflate, you know? They sit in their recliners watching daytime television until they don't even know what day of the week it is anymore. Hector can be a bit like that sometimes, honestly, if I don't drag him out to the hardware store with me. 

But I've always been a busybody. Even now, Maria is always telling me I have too many projects going on at once. Just this past Tuesday, for example, I was out in the garage until almost nine o'clock at night organizing my socket wrenches. I've got this old Craftsman set—the good kind they used to make back in the eighties before they moved all the manufacturing overseas—and I was building a custom wooden tray for them out of some scrap mahogany I had left over from when I fixed the trim in the hallway last spring. Took me hours to get the measurements exactly right so they wouldn't rattle around when you opened the drawer. So I'm certainly never lacking for things to occupy my time. 

And when I'm eating like that, in the middle of the night... it's not like I'm just sitting around twiddling my thumbs, looking for an activity. Usually, I've already read my book for the evening. Right now I'm reading a very thick biography of Teddy Roosevelt—fascinating man, really, the sheer amount of energy he had is just astounding to read about—and I'm genuinely trying to wind down and get some rest. 

I know what boredom feels like, Doctor. I remember being stuck at the DMV for four hours back in 2012 just to renew my license because their entire computer system crashed right after they called my number. That was boredom. You're just sitting there, staring at the linoleum, desperate for anything to happen. But this? This isn't that. I'm not looking for something to do. It's more like... my brain just suddenly locks onto the idea of the food, the tamales or the bread, and it just won't let go. It doesn't matter how busy I kept myself that day, or how many projects I have lined up for the next morning. So, no, I really don't think it has anything to do with being bored. I wish it were that simple, I really do. Then maybe I could just take up knitting or crossword puzzles and be done with it! But no, it's definitely not boredom.
Do you feel like you are unable to control your eating during these episodes, even if you want to stop?

Control... yes, Doctor, that is exactly it. That is the crux of the whole issue, really, and it’s the main thing that finally convinced me I needed to come in and talk to a professional. 

You see, I've always prided myself on being a disciplined man. Back at the shipping yard, you had to be. You couldn't just wander off or lose focus when a freighter was waiting to be unloaded and you had heavy machinery moving all around you. And even now, with my woodworking and my tools out in the garage... I measure twice, cut once, just like my father taught me when I was a boy. I have control over my hands, over my actions. I'm a careful, deliberate person in just about every other aspect of my life. 

But when it comes to this... these late-night trips to the kitchen... it's entirely different. What brings me in is that once I start picking at the leftovers late at night—whether it’s Maria’s tamales or maybe some roast chicken we had for Sunday dinner—it feels like there are two different people operating inside me. The sensible part of me, the part that organizes the socket wrenches and balances the checkbook every month, is sitting there saying, "That’s enough, Alejandro. You’ve had plenty, put the Tupperware away and go back to bed." It's loud and clear in my mind. I hear it. I genuinely want to stop. 

But my hand... it just keeps going back for more anyway. It’s like it has a mind of its own. I'll tell myself, "Okay, just one more bite," and then I swallow it, and before I can even turn around to close the refrigerator door, my hand is reaching right back into the container. It's the most baffling, frustrating thing in the world. I'll be standing there in my slippers—the good sheepskin ones Hector bought me for my birthday last year, which are wonderful on that cold kitchen tile, by the way—just watching my own hand ferry food to my mouth while my brain is practically yelling at me to stop. 

So yes, the control is just completely gone in those moments. I want to stop, I really do, but I just can't seem to make my body listen to reason once I've started.
Do you usually feel uncomfortably full after these late-night eating episodes?

Uncomfortably full... oh, absolutely. I mean, I don't usually get sick, thank goodness. My stomach has always been pretty ironclad—I remember back in the shipping yard, I could eat a spicy chili dog from the lunch truck at noon and go right back to lifting crates without a second thought. 

But this... this is entirely different. It’s not a sick feeling like I’m going to throw up, but it is just this... this immense, heavy pressure. I'll have eaten so much of whatever it is I found in the fridge that my belt—it's this thick leather one Maria bought me at a craft fair down in Sedona about five years ago, very sturdy, nice brass buckle—it just feels incredibly tight, digging right into my waist. I'll actually have to undo the buckle a notch or two just to get some relief and take a proper breath. 

And then... well, I can't just go right back to bed feeling like that. If I try to lie flat on the mattress, the pressure is just unbearable. So instead, I have to sort of shuffle my way out to the garage and just sit in my workshop chair for a good long while. It's this old, beat-up vinyl office chair I salvaged from a yard sale down the street—very comfortable, though the left armrest is a bit loose and I keep meaning to tighten the screws on it—and I just sit there in the dark. I'll sit there for maybe half an hour, sometimes forty-five minutes, just waiting for things to settle down because my stomach is so incredibly uncomfortable. It just feels stretched to the absolute limit, you know? Like a balloon that's got too much air in it. So, yes, "uncomfortably full" is exactly what happens.

You already ate, you don't need this, just close the door and go to bed." I hear that voice in my head so clearly. But my hand just keeps going back for more anyway. patient.answer:
Stressed? No, I... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, it’s quite the opposite, if you can believe it. You see, since I retired—and I worked for, oh, thirty-five years, always on the go, always some deadline or someone needing something from me—but now? Now there’s really nothing to be stressed about. The house is quiet, the bills are sorted. My evenings are... well, they’re incredibly peaceful. 

I usually just sit in my favorite armchair, it's this old leather one right by the window, and I might put on a history program or read a bit of whatever biography I've picked up from the library. patient.answer:
Guilty? Hmm. I... well, I don't know if I would use the word guilty, exactly. When I think of guilt, you know, I think about doing something wrong to somebody else. Like back when I was working, if I missed a deadline and caused a headache for the people in my department, or, oh, if I forget to call my sister on her birthday—that sort of thing makes me feel terribly guilty. But with this, it is just me in my own kitchen. I bought the groceries, it is my house, I am not taking food out of anyone else's mouth. So, no, I wouldn't say guilt. 

It is more just... well, it is a profound sense of bafflement, really. I will finish picking at whatever it is, and I will put the lid back on the container. I always make sure to press all the corners down tight, because there is nothing worse than refrigerator air drying out the leftovers, and then I will wash whatever fork or spoon I used. I always wash it and dry it right then and there, put it back in the drawer, and wipe down the counter with a sponge. I feel a bit foolish, I suppose. And, well, maybe a little physically heavy, because my stomach was already perfectly satisfied from my actual dinner. But I don't feel guilty like I have committed a crime. I just turn off the kitchen light, walk down the hall to my bedroom, and lay there in the dark for a while, just wondering why my brain and my hands do not seem to be on the same page. It is just so nonsensical, you know? I just go to sleep feeling completely confused about the whole routine.

When I really stop and think about it, the sheer volume of it all... If my daughter came over for dinner, I’d have one tamale, maybe some rice and beans, and that would be it. I’d be perfectly satisfied. patient.answer:
Ashamed... well, I don't know. I really don't know if I'd use that exact word. I don't feel like a criminal in my own kitchen, I just... well, I feel profoundly frustrated with myself, I suppose. 

I'll be standing there, looking down at the empty Tupperware—usually the one with the blue lid, because Maria always uses the blue-lidded ones for the heavy sauces like the mole so they don't stain the clear plastic—and I just look at it and think, 'Alejandro, what on earth are you doing?' It’s more of a complete bafflement. A real annoyance. I mean, I worked for nearly forty years managing logistics down at the shipping yard, keeping track of hundreds of moving parts, making sure every crate was exactly where it needed to be, right on schedule. I was a man who prided himself on discipline and order. 

So to find myself standing out in the cold garage, brushing pan dulce crumbs off my flannel shirt in the dark so my cousin Hector doesn't see them if he happens to walk out to use the washing machine... I don't know if I'd call it shame, exactly, but it is certainly a massive blow to my pride. It just doesn't make any sense to me. I do try to wash the containers quietly and put them in the drying rack before I go to bed, just so Maria doesn't wake up and see that all the leftovers are gone, but that's mostly because I just don't want her to worry or think she needs to cook even more food for us. So, I don't know if I have that deep feeling of shame you're talking about, or if it's just this intense irritation that I can't seem to manage my own two hands when the sun goes down.

patient.answer:
Fast? Well, you know, I haven't really stopped to think about the speed of it. It's an interesting question, though. When I'm out there in the garage, or standing by the counter with the blue-lidded Tupperware, the whole experience is just so... so strange. I've told you how it feels like I'm watching myself do it, like I'm not really the one in the driver's seat, even though my hands are the ones moving the food to my mouth. 

But as for how fast I'm eating... I really couldn't say. I don't think I'm shoveling it in like a man who hasn't seen a meal in three days, if that's what you mean. I mean, Maria's cooking is something to be savored, usually. Her mole, the way she toasts the chilies and grinds the chocolate... it takes her hours, sometimes a whole afternoon, just to get the balance right. You don't just inhale something that took that much care to prepare. Even the pan dulce, the conchas with the pink sugar topping, I usually like to break off a piece and have it with my coffee in the morning, taking my time with it while I read the paper. 

So when these episodes happen at night, with Hector watching his programs in the other room... I don't know that I'm racing through it. It's more about the sheer volume, the fact that I just keep going and going until the container is empty, rather than trying to beat some sort of clock. I'm just standing there, feeling that frustration I mentioned, wondering why I can't just put the lid back on. But the actual pace of the eating? I really haven't paid much attention to whether it's fast or slow. It just feels... relentless, I suppose is the best word for it. It just keeps happening until it's gone.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a lack of control and marked distress after the episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel distressed after these episodes, like something is wrong with your behavior?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling distressed regarding the binge eating episodes (which corresponds to marked distress, a specific diagnostic criterion), but this is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Distressed... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly the word for it. It's a very heavy feeling, you know? Like I said earlier about the frustration, it just... it sits with me. 

I'll be standing there in the garage, the washing machine humming quietly in the corner—it’s an older model, a Maytag, we’ve had it for maybe fifteen years and it still runs like a top, though it makes this slight rattling noise during the spin cycle that I’ve been meaning to look into. But anyway, I'll be standing there, and the last of the pan dulce is gone, and I look down at my hands, and this overwhelming sense of... of distress just washes over me. 

It’s not just that I ate too much. It’s this deep, unsettling feeling that something is fundamentally wrong with how I'm acting. I mean, I’m sixty-five years old. I should be well past the age of sneaking around my own house like a teenager trying to hide a bad report card. I spent my whole life being the responsible one, the one who planned the routes, the one who made sure the bills were paid on time, the one who fixed the leaky faucet before it became a real problem. And now, I can't even stop myself from eating a whole tray of tamales when I'm not even hungry. 

It just feels so out of character. It’s distressing because it doesn't align with who I know myself to be. I'll go back inside, quietly lock the door behind me so it doesn't click too loudly and wake Maria, and I'll just lie there in bed staring at the ceiling fan—we keep it on low, even in the winter, just to keep the air moving—and I just turn it over and over in my mind. Why did I do that? What is wrong with me that I can't just go to sleep like a normal person? It’s a very distressing loop to be caught in, Doctor. It really is. It makes me feel like I'm losing my grip on the steering wheel, if that makes sense.

Pleasure? Euphoria? Oh, no, no. I wouldn't say that at all. It's funny you use the word euphoria, actually. It makes me think of... well, years ago, when I was still working down at the shipping yard, we had this young fellow, maybe twenty-two, who won a scratch-off lottery ticket on his lunch break. Won about five thousand dollars, if I recall correctly. Now, that boy was euphoric. He was jumping up and down, buying everyone sodas from the machine in the breakroom—the old machine that always ate your quarters if you didn't push the button fast enough. That's euphoria. 

But what I'm doing out there in the garage, or standing in the kitchen in the dark? There's no joy in it. No pleasure. I mean, the food tastes good, of course. Maria is a wonderful cook. Her tamales, the ones she makes for Christmas with the pork shoulder she slow-roasts all day... they're delicious. And the pan dulce from the bakery down on 4th Street, the one with the green awning that's been there since before Hector and I were born—it's sweet, it's comforting. But when I'm eating it during these... these episodes, I'm not enjoying it. I'm not savoring it like I would if I were sitting at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning with a hot cup of coffee and the newspaper spread out in front of me.

It's more like... like a compulsion, I suppose. A drive. I'm just putting it in my mouth, chewing, swallowing, reaching for the next piece. I'm not thinking about the flavor or the texture. I'm not feeling happy or satisfied. If anything, it's just this dull, numbing sensation. Like I'm just trying to fill a hole, or quiet some sort of noise in my head, though I couldn't tell you what that noise is. It's just... I just have to do it, and I can't seem to stop until it's gone. And then, like I was saying before, the distress sets in. The frustration. But during the actual eating? No, doctor, there's no pleasure in it. It's just a mechanical, relentless sort of thing. I wish I could say it was enjoyable, at least then maybe it would make a little more sense to me, why I keep doing it. But it's not. It really isn't.

patient.answer:
Coping with emotions... well, you see, that's the thing that really stumps me about all of this. If you had asked me that back when I was still working down at the shipping yard—oh, say, fifteen or twenty years ago, right around the time they brought in all that new management and completely overhauled the scheduling system—I might have said yes. Back then, there was plenty of stress to go around. You'd come home with your shoulders pulled tight up to your ears, just completely worn down by the demands of the day and the foremen yelling over the noise of the machinery. 

But now? I'm sixty-five years old, Doctor. I'm retired. My days are... well, they're very peaceful, mostly. I get up, I have my coffee, Maria and I might go down to the market, or I'll spend some time tinkering out in the garage. Just last week I finally got around to replacing the spark plug on the lawnmower. It’s a Toro, a very reliable machine usually, but it gets a bit temperamental if it sits too long over the winter without being run. It took me a good hour to get it cleaned up and running smooth again. But anyway, the point I'm trying to make is that I don't really have a lot of... of turmoil in my life right now. 

I'm not sad. I'm not angry about anything. Hector and I get along just fine, even if he does play his television programs a bit too loud in the evenings—he's a little hard of hearing in his left ear from his time in the service, though you can't ever get him to admit it or go to a doctor for it. Life is good. So I don't feel like I'm trying to cope with anything when I'm out there eating. There's no big sadness or worry that I'm trying to push down with the food. 

When I'm standing there in the dark, I'm not thinking about my feelings at all. It's only after the fact that the emotions really hit me, that terrible distress and frustration I was telling you about earlier. But before it happens? Or during? I really haven't noticed any particular feeling or stress I'm trying to manage. It's just... a blank, really. I wish I could say, "Yes, Doctor, I'm stressed about the bills, and that's why I'm eating," because then at least it would make some logical sense. But I just don't see a connection like that.

patient.answer:
Boredom? Oh, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it's a perfectly fair question, I suppose, what with me being retired and all. I know a lot of fellows, when they finally leave the workforce, they just sort of deflate, you know? They sit in their recliners watching daytime television until they don't even know what day of the week it is anymore. Hector can be a bit like that sometimes, honestly, if I don't drag him out to the hardware store with me. 

But I've always been a busybody. Even now, Maria is always telling me I have too many projects going on at once. Just this past Tuesday, for example, I was out in the garage until almost nine o'clock at night organizing my socket wrenches. I've got this old Craftsman set—the good kind they used to make back in the eighties before they moved all the manufacturing overseas—and I was building a custom wooden tray for them out of some scrap mahogany I had left over from when I fixed the trim in the hallway last spring. Took me hours to get the measurements exactly right so they wouldn't rattle around when you opened the drawer. So I'm certainly never lacking for things to occupy my time. 

And when I'm eating like that, in the middle of the night... it's not like I'm just sitting around twiddling my thumbs, looking for an activity. Usually, I've already read my book for the evening. Right now I'm reading a very thick biography of Teddy Roosevelt—fascinating man, really, the sheer amount of energy he had is just astounding to read about—and I'm genuinely trying to wind down and get some rest. 

I know what boredom feels like, Doctor. I remember being stuck at the DMV for four hours back in 2012 just to renew my license because their entire computer system crashed right after they called my number. That was boredom. You're just sitting there, staring at the linoleum, desperate for anything to happen. But this? This isn't that. I'm not looking for something to do. It's more like... my brain just suddenly locks onto the idea of the food, the tamales or the bread, and it just won't let go. It doesn't matter how busy I kept myself that day, or how many projects I have lined up for the next morning. So, no, I really don't think it has anything to do with being bored. I wish it were that simple, I really do. Then maybe I could just take up knitting or crossword puzzles and be done with it! But no, it's definitely not boredom.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's late-night eating episodes are accompanied by a lack of self-control

patient.answer:
Control... yes, Doctor, that is exactly it. That is the crux of the whole issue, really, and it’s the main thing that finally convinced me I needed to come in and talk to a professional. 

You see, I've always prided myself on being a disciplined man. Back at the shipping yard, you had to be. You couldn't just wander off or lose focus when a freighter was waiting to be unloaded and you had heavy machinery moving all around you. And even now, with my woodworking and my tools out in the garage... I measure twice, cut once, just like my father taught me when I was a boy. I have control over my hands, over my actions. I'm a careful, deliberate person in just about every other aspect of my life. 

But when it comes to this... these late-night trips to the kitchen... it's entirely different. What brings me in is that once I start picking at the leftovers late at night—whether it’s Maria’s tamales or maybe some roast chicken we had for Sunday dinner—it feels like there are two different people operating inside me. The sensible part of me, the part that organizes the socket wrenches and balances the checkbook every month, is sitting there saying, "That’s enough, Alejandro. You’ve had plenty, put the Tupperware away and go back to bed." It's loud and clear in my mind. I hear it. I genuinely want to stop. 

But my hand... it just keeps going back for more anyway. It’s like it has a mind of its own. I'll tell myself, "Okay, just one more bite," and then I swallow it, and before I can even turn around to close the refrigerator door, my hand is reaching right back into the container. It's the most baffling, frustrating thing in the world. I'll be standing there in my slippers—the good sheepskin ones Hector bought me for my birthday last year, which are wonderful on that cold kitchen tile, by the way—just watching my own hand ferry food to my mouth while my brain is practically yelling at me to stop.

Uncomfortably full... oh, absolutely. I mean, I don't usually get sick, thank goodness. My stomach has always been pretty ironclad—I remember back in the shipping yard, I could eat a spicy chili dog from the lunch truck at noon and go right back to lifting crates without a second thought.
